20   Q.   WHAT IS THE PURPOSE OF YOUR TESTIMONY?

21   A.   In my testimony, I will comment on EPE’s proposal to completely abandon the long-standing

22        Commission practice of rate mitigation and stability through banding and gradualism.

23        Because the NMDOJ does not have a specific total overall revenue requirement

24        recommendation in this case, I look instead at various scenarios for the overall increase in

25        base revenues, which are used for illustrative purposes in order to show my proposed banding

26        approach. For the various overall base-revenue increase scenarios, my banding approach is

27        shown to be consistent with past Commission decisions. Finally, I will comment on EPE’s

28        proposed residential standard-service rate design, with special attention to the residential

 1   Q.       PLEASE EXPLAIN WHAT YOU MEAN BY THE “MAXIMUM BAND” IN TABLE

 2            DG-1.

 3                     The maximum band refers to the percentage that is multiplied by the overall base

 4            revenue percent increase. This multiplication yields the maximum base-revenue percent

 5            increase – or cap – for an individual rate class. Typically, the maximum band is greater than

 6            100%, meaning that the resulting cap is greater than the overall percent increase. For example,

 7            Table DG-1 shows that in the Final Order issued in PNM Case No. 24-00089-UT, the

 8            Maximum Band was 143.89% and the total overall base revenue increase was 13.8%.

 9            Therefore, Residential customers, being subject to the maximum band, received a base-

10            revenue percent increase equal to 143.84% * 13.8% = 19.85% (or put another way, 1.4384 *

11            13.8 = 19.85). The maximum percent increase (or cap) is applied to those classes that would

12            have received a percent increase greater than the cap under full-cost base-revenue

13            allocations. 7 On the other hand, the minimum band refers to the percentage that – once

14            multiplied by the overall percent increase – yields the minimum base-revenue percent increase

15            – or floor – for an individual rate class. Typically, the minimum band is less than 100%. The

16            minimum percent increase (or floor) is applied to those classes that would have received a

17            percent increase less than the floor under full-cost allocations. Typically, the classes at the cap

18            are referred to as “subsidized classes” while classes at the floor are referred to as “subsidizing

19            classes.”

20                     While the determination of specific maximum band involves some subjective

21            judgement, it is generally agreed that in cases with lower overall base revenue percent

14                    [The] history shows that gradualism has not moved customers meaningfully to full

17                    not resulting in customers being near full cost rates supports that it is better to start at
18                    full cost rates consistent with EPE’s proposal to allocate revenue by rate class at full

20                    than continuing the moderation practice, this full cost proposal limits rate recovery
21                    below the actual cost of providing service and having some rate classes subsidize
22                    others. In this rate case, EPE is putting forth the recommendation to move rate classes
23                    to the full recovery of their respective cost of service, thereby eliminating inter-class
24                    subsidies. Any rate mitigation and stability through banding and gradualism will
25                    remain solely within the Commission’s purview.

 4   Q.      WHAT IS MEANT BY AFFORDABILITY?

 5   A.      Household affordability includes whether or not proposed residential customers’ revenue and

 6           rate increases are reasonably absorbable by households – especially in light of price increases

 7           for other goods and services purchased by household. Similarly, business affordability

 8           includes whether or not the proposed business (primarily small businesses) customers’

 9           revenue and rate increases are reasonably absorbable. In its response to Staff’s Interrogatory

10           and Request for Production Staff 3-1, EPE also notes that common regulatory usage of

11           affordability includes an evaluation of “the extent to which a good or service is priced for a

12           person or household to buy it without compromising the ability to pay for other basic

13           necessities.”

 3   Q.   ARE THERE OTHER TYPES OF FIXED COSTS BESIDES CUSTOMER-RELATED

 4        COSTS?

 5   A.   Yes. In a cost-of-service study, costs that do not vary with kWh are typically deemed to be

 6        “fixed costs.” These fixed costs are comprised of customer-related costs as well as demand-

 7        related costs, or, capacity-related costs. Demand-related costs are sensitive to the demands –

 8        measured as kW of load – placed on the system, which affect the amount of generation and line

 9        capacity required to satisfy these loads. While both are considered fixed costs, the key

10        distinction between customer-related costs and demand-related costs is that demand-related

11        costs are sensitive to the utility serving customers’ loads (peak and average), while customer-

12        related costs are sensitive to simply connecting a customer to the network irrespective of the

13        customer’s load or kWh usage.

14   Q.   IF DEMAND-RELATED COSTS ARE “FIXED” THEN SHOULDN’T THEY BE

15        RECOVERED THROUGH THE CUSTOMER CHARGE?

16   A.   No. Both demand-related and customer-related costs are conventionally viewed as being

17        “fixed” in that they are viewed as not being sensitive to producing kWh of energy. The two cost

18        classifications, however, are sensitive to completely different services provided by the utility;

19        therefore, it is inappropriate to simply comingle them into the same “fixed-cost” category and

20        essentially treat them as the same type of cost for rate-design purposes. Demand-related costs

21        are sensitive to the utility serving customers’ loads, while customer-related costs are sensitive

22        to simply connecting a customer to the network irrespective of the customer’s kW load or kWh

23        usage.   Moreover, there is typically a strong positive correlation between monthly kWh

 5        setting the customer charge include such concerns as gradualism, incentivizing energy
